newsitem.title: CHINA: China state debt selling well despite low rate.
newsitem.headline: China state debt selling well despite low rate.

text.p: China's latest batch of state debt has been selling well despite a low coupon rate, but it is unlikely to do much to boost activity on the slow secondary state debt spot market, analysts said on Monday.

A total of 40 billion yuan ($4.82 billion) worth of three-year tradable treasury notes is being issued from May 1 to May 30, of which more than 50 percent has so far been sold, brokers and bankers estimated.

The annual interest rate for the new issue was set at 9.18 percent, much lower than the average yield of over 10 percent for existing contracts on Shanghai's state debt spot market, which accounts for more than 95 percent of trading nationwide.

"The note is selling well partly because it will be listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges after the issue," said one state debt investment analyst with a major Chinese securities houses.

"Investors believe the new batch signals more tradable state debt will be issued over the rest of this year," said a second analyst. "They are buying the new debt expecting it to perform well after listing."

Beijing announced in February that it would issue 123 billion yuan in non-tradable T-notes of two years, three years and five years duration from March 1 to October 20. That batch has not sold as well as the new batch, brokers said.

But traders said they did not expect the popularity of the new T-note to help revive trading on the secondary state debt spot market, which has been hard hit in recent months with liquidity flowing into the booming stock markets.
Daily volume of the spot market in Shanghai has fallen to around one million lots on average from around 1.5 million lots a few months ago, traders said.
One lot is 1,000 yuan face value of state debt.

"The stock markets are likely to continue their bull run at least until early July when China takes over Hong Kong," one trader said. "That will prevent investors putting more money into existing contracts on the secondary spot market including this new batch of T-notes."

"The good sales on the primary (state debt issue) market will not have a great impact on the secondary spot market," said a second trader. "The spot market is likely to be neglected at least until the second quarter of this year."
Analysts said the good sales of the new batch of state debt was also a result of growing bank deposits and a lack of alternative investment channels other than the stock markets.

China plans to issue a record 248.596 billion yuan worth of domestic and foreign debt this year, mainly to cover state budget deficits and redeem maturing debt. Last year, it issued a historical high of 195.2 billion yuan in state debt.
More than 99 percent worth of China's state debt issues so far have been domestic. ($1 = 8.293 yuan)
